title: Debate
hookLine: monks in the courtyard debate with a clap and a stamp

lines: A SLAP, A STAMP, A QUESTION.
cards: Crack. The sound comes over the monastery wall like a branch snapping. Then another, then laughter.

Inside, in a shaded courtyard, monks in maroon robes are scattered in small groups. In each one a monk sits on the ground, calm. Another stands over him, rosary looped on his arm, and fires a question.
Then he swings his right hand high, slaps it down against his left palm, and stamps his foot. The seated monk answers. Nobody here is angry.
This is how they study. Today: debate.

teach.b: First, the roles. In Tibetan monastic debate, the defender sits and holds a position.
The challenger stands and tests it, asking question after question until either the position holds or the defender contradicts what he said a minute ago.
Second, the clap and the stamp. Each time the challenger makes a point, he claps, right hand down onto the left palm, and stamps. It wakes everyone up.

Teachers give the gesture meanings of their own; one explanation is that the clap cuts through confusion, the way a point lands. Tradition says debates open by calling on Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom.
Third, the rules of answering. The defender doesn't make speeches. He answers from a small set of formal replies, roughly: I accept.

teach.h: I ACCEPT. NOT ESTABLISHED. DOESN'T FOLLOW.
teach.b: It doesn't follow. Every answer has to be exact, and a careless yes can be turned against him a few questions later. Students practice this for years, working through logic, the stages of the path and the nature of mind.

Fourth, why a contemplative tradition shouts. Tibetan teachers say understanding that hasn't been tested is just borrowed. Debate shows whether a student actually understands emptiness or only remembers the words.

teach.h: TEST THE VIEW, NOT THE PERSON.
teach.b: And the aim is the view, not the person: monks who were slapping and stamping at each other an hour ago walk to dinner together.
The goal isn't to win. It's to see clearly. In year three you met a very different debate, at Samye, where a king chose.
This one happens every day, between friends.

how: In Tibetan monastic colleges, students debate daily in courtyards: a standing challenger questions a seated defender with a characteristic clap and stamp, and the defender replies from a small set of formal answers, as a way of testing and deepening understanding of the texts.

o: testing the teaching through questions, claps and stamps
a contest where monks argue to shame their rivals
a silent retreat where students study texts alone

Tibetan teachers say understanding should be tested

games.q: you're the defender. the challenger's question seems easy, and a quick yes would end it. what do you do?
o: say yes fast and move on.
answer exactly, since a careless yes can be turned against you later.
games.why: every answer must be exact; a careless yes can return a few questions later as a contradiction.

practice: Pick something you believe without having checked it lately, about a person, about yourself, about the way things are, and say it in one plain sentence.

Then stand up inside as the challenger and ask it honest questions: how do I know that? Does that always follow? You don't need to change your mind; just see where the reasoning is solid and where it's borrowed.

wordCard.voice: Debate. In Tibetan monasteries, a seated defender and a standing challenger test the teaching with questions, claps and stamps, to understand, not to win. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit vada, debate or discussion; Tibetan monastic debate continues the Indian Buddhist tradition of reasoned argument.

carryVoice: Your line: clap and ask. Test the view hard, and never the person. That's today, done.
